item.title: Trump Asked Musk to Reverse Limits on Ukraine’s Military Internet Use
item.description:
President Trump called Elon Musk last week and asked him to restore Ukraine’s full access to the Starshield satellite communications network, according to a senior administration official and a person briefed on the exchange.

Mr. Trump’s call to Mr. Musk, who owns the Starshield network, came after Ukrainian officials reported that they were encountering new limits on their ability to operate the military drones that have become essential to their war against Russia. The development raised alarms in Ukraine that Mr. Trump, who has demanded that Ukraine stop its drone attacks on Russian diesel refineries, might have instructed Mr. Musk to impose the limits.

Asked on Thursday whether he had made such a call to Mr. Musk, as first reported by The Wall Street Journal, Mr. Trump declined to say. “I don’t want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether ⁠somebody else called — doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line — he put it back,” the president ​told reporters.

When asked for comment, the White House pointed to Mr. Trump’s remarks.

It remained unclear on Thursday whether access to the Starshield network had been fully restored. Some Ukrainian officials said that was not yet the case.

But supporters of Ukraine were cautiously optimistic.

“If these reports are true, this is a welcome development,” Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, posted on X. Mr. Tillis said it remained unclear who, if anyone, had made the initial decision to throttle Ukraine’s Starshield access. But he said that anyone who objects to its restoration should “have the courage to raise your hand, and explain your justification for allowing Putin to continue to mow down toddlers in strollers in Ukrainian parks.”

The issue emerged when Ukrainian drones began dropping from the sky in mid-October. Ukrainian commanders discovered that drones flown against Russian targets at high speeds were suddenly losing their connection to Starshield, a military version of the Starlink satellite communications network owned by Mr. Musk. Ukraine relies heavily on Starshield to operate its drones and for other military purposes as it battles Russia.

The restrictions came without warning or explanation. But Mr. Trump recently demanded that Kyiv halt its drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, which have helped cause diesel prices to surge ahead of the midterm elections. That has led Ukrainian officials and backers of the country to suspect that Mr. Trump might have been looking to constrain or even punish Kyiv for continuing those attacks.

The episode has confused Ukrainian officials and supporters of the country in Washington, and much uncertainty remains. Here is a look at some of the key questions involved.

Starshield is the military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s popular satellite internet service. SpaceX, the rocket and artificial intelligence company run by Mr. Musk, says that Starshield is “designed to support U.S. national defense use cases for the Department of Defense and other government partners.” The company says that Starshield offers a higher level of encryption and security than Starlink, allowing for the secure transmission of classified information.

The U.S. government has spent billions of dollars on the technology, and has granted Ukrainian forces access to the network. While Ukraine uses both Starlink and Starshield for internet connection on the battlefield, its leaders say that Starshield is particularly vital because it offers clearer communication at faster speeds than Starlink, along with higher security.

Like Starlink, Starshield relies on satellites in low earth orbit that have been launched into space by SpaceX’s proprietary rockets. SpaceX said that Starlink relies on more than 6,750 satellites currently in orbit, though it has not disclosed how many satellites are used by Starshield.

Starshield users on earth use satellite dishes, also known as terminals, to receive a signal from the satellites, which is then broadcast as high-speed internet. Devices, whether they are computers or drones, can then connect to that internet signal.

Mr. Musk’s technology has been valuable to Ukraine because Russian attacks since Moscow’s February 2022 invasion of the country have badly damaged much of Ukraine’s communications infrastructure.

This is the crucial question, and one with an unclear answer.

Mr. Musk has long insisted that the Defense Department makes decisions about the use of Starshield. He doubled down on that assessment last week after facing criticism for Ukraine’s connectivity restrictions.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he wrote on X, referring to an acronym for the president of the United States.

But Secretary of State Marco Rubio seemed to say the opposite this week. The United States “cannot direct a private company,” he told reporters on Wednesday, adding that neither Mr. Trump nor anyone else “in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”

Mr. Rubio chided Ukrainian officials for suggesting otherwise. He also insisted that the Trump administration was not made aware in advance of any new Starshield restrictions.

Appearing on “Fox & Friends” on Thursday, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said that Mr. Rubio — who as a U.S. senator from Florida ardently supported Ukraine’s fight against Russia — had told him in a Wednesday phone conversation that the State Department was working to “unblock” Starlink connectivity in Ukraine.

Another open question is whether SpaceX, which built Starshield for the Pentagon, retains access to its devices after they are handed over to the U.S. government. Mr. Musk did not respond to a request for comment.

Ukrainian troops have found that their drones can no longer fly faster than 100 miles per hour without losing their Starshield connection. In some cases, drones fell from the sky.

While many pilots operating short-range drones were able to resume work at lower speeds, many other operations rely on drones that must fly faster to avoid detection. Those operations were halted, disrupted or delayed, commanders said, as Ukraine urgently sought workarounds to avoid Russian advances.

Russian troops, aware of the sudden disappearance of many longer-range drones, began moving more freely along routes where Ukrainian drones typically attack, commanders and officials said. Starshield does not work in Russia, so the sudden slowdown did not affect any cross-border operations, including any planned strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, officials said. Instead, it hampered vulnerable frontline troops.

It also reduced Ukraine’s ability to intercept the jet-powered drones terrorizing major cities in the country, including Kyiv, Mr. Zelensky said. Not all Ukrainian interception systems rely on Starshield, but those that do must be able to outrace the Russian drones, which move faster than 100 miles per hour.

The disruption to Ukrainian military operations has not been enough to change the course of the war, which has largely been at a stalemate for more than four years along a front in Ukraine’s east.

But Ukrainian officials and their supporters in the West are as worried as they have ever been about whether Mr. Trump may withdraw U.S. support for Ukraine, which includes military intelligence sharing that is vital to Ukrainian operations.

Mr. Trump has taken several steps that favor Russia in recent weeks, including striking an agreement with Russia’s president, Vladimir V. Putin, to purchase Russian diesel fuel. Mr. Trump also recently exempted Russia from a major new sanctions package passed by Congress.

Mr. Trump has also begun a new push to broker a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, something he has long promised to deliver. He has sharply criticized Mr. Zelensky for what he calls the Ukrainian leader’s unwillingness to make peace with Mr. Putin, even though many Western diplomats and analysts argue that Mr. Putin has not offered peace terms that Mr. Zelensky could reasonably be expected to accept.

Mr. Trump’s envoys to Russia, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are also now discussing potential lucrative business deals between the United States and Russia as part of a settlement.

Many Ukrainian officials fear that the Starshield outage may reflect a broader Trump administration tilt toward Russia as it seeks to fulfill Mr. Trump’s promise to end the war.

item.title: Students at an A.I. School Were Supposed to Learn Faster. Many Aren’t.
item.description:
Alpha School, a fast-growing network of expensive private schools, promises to use A.I. to teach kids twice as much as they would learn in a traditional classroom in half the time. Academics take just two to three morning hours on a computer, freeing up the afternoons for workshops on vibe-coding, public speaking and sports.

The Trump administration has promoted Alpha as a model for “harnessing A.I.” to prepare tomorrow’s work force. Business leaders are talking it up on social media and podcasts, and some have signed up their own children.

For now, Alpha is a small, for-profit network, with lots of buzz and powerful backers, including the software billionaire Joe Liemandt. Its private schools serve about 1,500 students across 50 campuses.

But Alpha has huge ambitions to reach one billion students worldwide through its proprietary “A.I tutor.”

The plan depends partly on extending its reach into public schools. Already, the Alpha software platform has been quietly adopted by several school districts in Texas and South Carolina, according to a company document reviewed by The New York Times. About 2,600 public school students are now using the software.

To reach more, Alpha needs to prove that its technology works for a broader range of children, beyond its core customer base of affluent, tech-enthusiast families. But as Alpha markets itself to districts and states, a growing number of educators, and former Alpha parents and employees, are questioning the effectiveness of the network’s high-tech, low-book model.

Most of the students enrolled at Alpha private schools, which charge as much as $75,000 per year, earn high test scores compared with peers in more typical schooling environments. Some parents say their children are thriving. Still, many Alpha private school students are not meeting the targets at the center of the company’s marketing.

About half of K-8 students enrolled in Alpha private schools last year did not meet the promise that they would learn math twice as fast, according to Alpha data reviewed by The New York Times. About a fifth of students, out of about 400 total, missed the goal in reading.

Less than half of students were able to double their rate of learning in both subjects, according to the data, which spans fall 2025 to early 2026.

Alpha students are participating, essentially, in an experiment. At Alpha, there are no traditional teachers, few books and little paper. All of the academic lessons are delivered via apps, and students can earn lavish prizes for completing their work. Adults are present, but only as motivational guides: Students stuck on a concept can do video calls with tutors abroad. Some children who struggle leave or have been pushed out, according to documents and several former private school parents and employees.

Pushing out students is not uncommon in private schools, but public education presents a new test for Alpha. Many of the public school students now using the company’s software are considered at risk academically. Their schools cannot remove them. And public schools will not have access to the same perks Alpha offers its private school students as incentives to work hard.

This article is based on a review of Alpha documents and statements made by its executives, along with interviews with nine current and former Alpha parents and employees across the country. Some parents asked to remain anonymous to protect their children’s privacy. The employees requested anonymity because they did not want to risk their ability to work in the field.

The documents obtained by The Times show for the first time how Alpha student performance — based on its internal data and metrics — measures up to Alpha’s promises to families, and the full extent of the network’s reach into public education.

A spokeswoman for Alpha School, Anna Davlantes, said the company would not respond to written questions or requests for on-the-record interviews. This week, a curriculum expert working with Alpha shared a blog post saying the network was developing new software and bringing books into the curriculum.

Alpha is riding a wave of fascination — and anxiety — with how artificial intelligence might transform learning. But its app-driven instruction cuts against the grain of a growing parent movement demanding fewer screens in classrooms. Research points to direct adult instruction, books and tactile materials as critical to effective learning.

In the Houston Independent School District, where two public schools are piloting the model, the superintendent, Mike Miles, said in the early weeks students spent longer than expected on the Alpha apps, eating into the time that was supposed to be spent on afternoon enrichment.

Still, Mr. Miles has rejected the idea of banning A.I. or screens entirely from schools. “We’re way behind on what kids need to know and be able to do to be successful in a different world and workplace,” he said.

But, he added, “I am a little skeptical for kids who struggle.”

MacKenzie Price, an Alpha founder, has said she was inspired to start the network in Austin, Texas, in 2014, after her own daughter complained she was bored at school. The program met in a private home, with a small group of students using mainstream learning apps.

But around 2022, when generative artificial intelligence broke out, Alpha changed focus. That is when Mr. Liemandt, whose children attended Alpha, began investing heavily in the school and its technology, he has said, with a goal of transforming education “for everybody in the world.”

Mr. Liemandt now holds the title of principal of Alpha School, and serves as the network’s de facto chief executive.

Ms. Price, meanwhile, became an influencer in tech and education as she talked about regular schools “doing it all wrong.” Her ideas attracted supporters like Linda McMahon, the education secretary, and Bill Ackman, the hedge fund manager.

Even Elizabeth Holmes, the imprisoned Theranos founder, has boosted the network, calling Ms. Price “a visionary.”

The vision is that students will “love school” and “crush academics,” learning “2x in two hours” online.

The product at the center of the model is TimeBack, Alpha’s software platform. Over 7,000 students in total are using TimeBack, according to an Alpha document. In addition to Alpha private school students and several thousand public school students, the platform delivers academics to home-schooled students, to students in Poland and Malawi, and to students whose tuition costs are paid for by the state of Texas through its new voucher program.

On the TimeBack platform, students are directed to lessons in core subjects, including English, math and science. Alpha markets the app as an innovative “A.I. tutor.” But it does not contain a chatbot.

A.I. appears mainly to work behind the scenes, analyzing student progress in a number of learning apps, some proprietary and some popular in traditional schools, according to a Times review of the software and interviews with parents.

The apps contain reading passages, comprehension questions and math problems, targeted to a student’s level.

Public schools everywhere have long used learning apps, usually for practice. But in the Alpha model, the apps are the delivery system for new material.

Alpha private schools employ classroom “guides,” whose job is to motivate students, not deliver lessons, according to job listings and current and former employees. Students stuck in the apps on a tricky concept — what Alpha leaders refer to as the “doom loop” — can book time with tutors. But as the network expands rapidly, they must sometimes wait several days to get help, people affiliated with Alpha said.

Students read some literary and primary source documents in the app, but A.I. also generates articles for students to read and writing exercises tailored to children’s interests — gymnastics, Harry Potter — and offers feedback on student prose.

Like many other learning apps, TimeBack makes academics feel like a game. It awards points, known as XP, when children complete certain goals, and ranks students by name on a digital leaderboard. Parents can track their children’s progress on an online dashboard.

But the Alpha experience, at least on its private campuses, is not limited to the software.

Alpha bills its technology as a timesaver, and students are supposed to use their afternoons for “life skills.” At the private campuses, that could mean lessons in stand-up comedy or starting small businesses, bespoke experiences that are not available to others using TimeBack.

Alpha also has a unique incentive system. At the private schools, students who finish their app sessions can sit next to friends or win stuffed toys and electronics. For longer-term goals, there are bigger rewards, like cross-country field trips. Students can also earn cash — up to $1,000 for high test scores, according to an Alpha document.

Sarah Cone, whose 8-year-old daughter is in her second year at Alpha’s site in Lower Manhattan, said her daughter mastered two years of academics in about one year.

Ms. Cone, who founded a venture capital firm, moved her child from an elite traditional private school to Alpha. She praised the way the program encouraged her daughter to follow her interests: joining a book club and working with peers to create a baking business. African drumming and robot-building workshops have been highlights. The school has a library, she added.

Unlike at other Alpha campuses, Manhattan students are registered with the city as home-schooled students, because the state’s Education Department declined to incorporate Alpha as a private school. At least six other states have rejected Alpha’s bids to open public charter schools, often raising questions about its lack of traditional teachers.

Ms. Cone said she was unbothered.

“She is extremely happy at Alpha and really learning,” she said of her daughter.

Edward Nevraumont relocated to Austin so his four children could attend an Alpha private school. He likes that he can track online how his children are doing and that they can accelerate beyond grade level. His daughter Everest was Melania Trump’s State of the Union guest.

Mr. Nevraumont said the curriculum could be thin but praised Alpha for being responsive to parent feedback. The biggest gap is depth in the humanities, he added: “Things like literature, history, geography, fine art, music.”

Most Alpha private school students are high performers. The median K-8 student scored at the 87th percentile nationally in math last winter on a widely used assessment, the MAP, and at the 89th percentile in reading.

Alpha’s academic commitment to parents is based on growth, however.

Between last fall and winter, a majority of students — 75 percent — advanced at least as fast as projected by national averages. But only 42 percent progressed twice as fast in both math and reading, meeting the “2x” growth standard featured in the company’s marketing.

Alpha had an especially difficult time meeting that mark for its lower-performing math students. About a fifth of Alpha’s private school students scored at or below the 50th percentile nationally in math last fall, and only 37 percent of that group met the network’s promised 2x growth by winter.

Alpha highlights network-wide averages, rather than student-level results. A curriculum expert working with Alpha, Karen Vaites, wrote in a blog post Thursday that the network’s earlier results “are based on a set of products that aren’t half as good as what we’re creating now.”

Experts caution that public school students using Alpha’s model may not perform as well as affluent private school students. Home environment heavily influences learning outcomes, and public school students will not have access to the same rewards system Alpha uses to motivate performance.

David Slifka said those incentives had worked for his 14-year-old twins, who are thriving at Alpha in New York after struggling to focus in traditional classrooms.

“It’s so hard to know what education should be like with the rise of A.I.,” Mr. Slifka said. “I don’t know that anybody has it figured out, including Alpha. But at least they’re working hard to try.”

Some Alpha families have left voluntarily, while others were pushed out after their children struggled socially or did not achieve certain academic growth metrics, according to documents and several former parents and employees.

Parents at the Alpha campus in Brownsville, Texas, have also reported high rates of student turnover, according to Wired.

A former employee who spent time on several campuses said Alpha staff had talked about how to balance a push to increase enrollment while also counseling out children who struggled.

Alpha does not publish student attrition data, but Tasha Arnold, an Alpha official, told the Boston School Committee in April that the network had 6 percent turnover.

In a video explaining Alpha’s learning model, Ms. Price, the network’s founder, emphasized that it works for most students, but not all.

“We believe that ed tech is only 10 percent of the solution, while 90 percent is having a motivated student,” she said. “It is a messy process. We tell parents to expect results, not polish.”

The paucity of physical books, paper and pencils stood out to Savannah Ngo, a reading specialist who visited one of Alpha’s California campuses last spring when she was interviewing for a job with the network — part of a new push by Alpha to hire educators with expertise in early literacy.

“It was unsettling,” she said of the experience.

During her visit, Ms. Ngo saw that students had been given bound volumes of stories they had composed. One child told Ms. Ngo he had prompted an A.I. chatbot to write the text. Chatbots can be used in afternoon workshops, though they are not part of the morning app-based curriculum.

Ms. Ngo was offered the job but turned it down, despite feeling that many of the staff she met were warm and committed.

Laura Tortorelli is a reading researcher at Michigan State University who is developing an A.I. reading app. She said that while technology can provide personalized practice, it cannot replace human teaching.

Research shows students comprehend more of what they read in print than on screens, she noted.

“I love ed tech,” she said. “I’m interested in its potential for helping teachers do their job better. Not replacing teachers.”

A former Alpha employee said classroom guides were energetic but often lacked formal education training. The employee saw students as young as 5 sitting alone as they struggled with tasks like forming letters. Children were sometimes directed to YouTube videos for help.

There is also new scrutiny on the student culture at Alpha.

Wayne Vaughan, a former Alpha parent, wrote this fall on social media that his son attended Alpha’s flagship elementary school in Austin for five years, where fellow parents reported “negative self talk” among their children because of the pressure created by being ranked against peers by name.

Private high school students across several Alpha campuses recently participated in an eight-week freshman “boot camp,” meant to build traits like grit and entrepreneurship. Among other tasks, they were asked to clean public bathrooms or perform other “dirty jobs.”

Some students were hooked up to heart-rate monitors while they watched videos of their parents critiquing them, in front of their peers.

“We do not think the existence of discomfort means the exercise has failed,” says an Alpha website describing the boot camp. “In fact, in many ways, it illustrates why this skill needs to be taught.”

Some boot camp students posted about the experience with enthusiasm, although at least one expressed apprehension.

The existence of the boot camp was revealed by Benjamin Riley, a longtime education policy expert who has become a vocal opponent of A.I. in schools.

The children of tech and finance executives are not the only ones learning with Alpha.

The network also includes Unbound Academy, a virtual public charter school in Arizona. The school has posted underwhelming academic results, according to program data.

And Alpha leaders are marketing TimeBack under the brand name Studient to traditional public schools, promising that districts will pay only for students who meet learning goals. One Alpha document shows nearly 2,000 students in South Carolina are using the software, in the Jasper County School District and Allendale County Schools. Officials in those districts did not respond to questions.

In Fort Davis, a rural Texas district, and the Aldine Independent School District, in Houston, subsets of students use TimeBack to supplement traditional instruction for fewer than two hours a day, according to district staff. Texas school districts using TimeBack said they were not paying for it.

A spokeswoman for the Aldine schools said successful students could choose prizes from a catalog, ranging from small toys to a bike.

Michelle Hartmann, the chief innovation officer in Fort Davis, wrote in an email, “It is an exciting time in Texas education when what used to be a Hard No becomes a Hell Yea!”

Texas state education officials facilitated discussions between school districts and Alpha, according to The Texas Tribune and ProPublica.

The public schools using TimeBack are predominantly Black, Hispanic and low-income.

In the Houston Independent School District, about 100 children were selected to pilot TimeBack for math and reading because they were performing above the 60th percentile. The program was supposed to free up time in the afternoon for field trips and other hands-on learning.

But according to Mr. Miles, the Houston superintendent, in the first five weeks, many students spent afternoons on catch-up.

In Alpha’s private schools, some students also spend far longer than two hours per day on TimeBack, and some families hire tutors, according to parents and employees.

Mr. Miles said families could exit the program, and the district would pull children who do not make sufficient progress.

Daniel Willingham, a cognitive psychologist at the University of Virginia, said he had serious concerns about Alpha’s methods. Compressing academics into two hours per day suggests a lack of breadth and depth, he said.

“They think the way you toughen kids up is to get them to clean a bathroom, and the way you get them to learn is to power through it as quickly as possible,” Professor Willingham said, adding, “These are naïve theories of psychology.”

Alex Klavens contributed reporting. Georgia Gee and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

I’ve been reporting on education for 20 years, and noticed that a for-profit network called Alpha School had some of the buzz that charter schools had when they first expanded nationally — a sense that a hugely innovative new education model was being introduced that could remake the landscape. But there have also been big questions about how Alpha uses artificial intelligence, and whether its student data lives up to its audacious marketing claim that kids will learn twice as much in half the time using an A.I. tutor.

item.title: He Put the Billionaire Tax on the Ballot. It Could Be His Last Stand.
item.description:
Late last year, Dave Regan, the pugnacious head of a California health care workers union, wanted his colleagues from other labor groups to support his politically explosive proposition to tax the assets of the state’s billionaires.

At a meeting in Los Angeles, he pulled aside Tia Orr, the executive director of the Service Employees International Union statewide council, to make himself clear.

“State Council better endorse this measure by January 1st or I’m coming for you,” Mr. Regan said, according to a report written by lawyers hired by S.E.I.U. to investigate accusations of intimidation. A copy of the report was obtained by The New York Times.

Mr. Regan has long been known for playing hardball and taking a go-it-alone approach to California politics as he has built power for his union, S.E.I.U.-United Healthcare Workers West. Along the way, he has made numerous enemies in California’s Democratic circles, even as he has pushed for liberal causes they might be inclined to support.

Besides facing multiple allegations of intimidation over the billionaire tax, Mr. Regan was recently accused of physically assaulting a former union director 17 years ago. A nurses union and several state lawmakers are calling for him to resign.

S.E.I.U. International, which oversees Mr. Regan’s union, plans a hearing into the allegations and could discipline him or remove him from his job.

The tumult comes during the highest-profile campaign of Mr. Regan’s career — a November ballot measure that could create the nation’s first wealth tax by targeting the assets of California’s billionaires and devoting the revenue to health care. The novel proposal, which would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires residing in the state, is backed by prominent liberal economists as well as national progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

Mr. Regan has denied the accusations of intimidation and assault. He said it was “categorically false” that he made any sort of threat against other labor leaders. He cast the assertions as a politically motivated smear campaign by opponents of the billionaire tax.

“When you take on billionaires and when you do things that powerful people don’t like, it comes with consequences,” he said.

In California, the billionaire tax initiative, Proposition 40, has driven a sharp wedge into Democratic politics. Labor unions are split, and Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes the tax measure, fearing that it would drive entrepreneurs and their tax dollars away from California.

For some, the man behind the plan is also part of the problem.

“It has been very ugly, very personal,” said Gale Kaufman, a veteran Democratic strategist in California who has long advised a powerful state teachers union.

Mr. Regan, she said in a recent public forum, “has single-handedly blown up coalitions that have been together on Democratic issues for years.”

Mr. Regan moved to California from Ohio in 2009 during an earlier era of conflict within S.E.I.U., one of the nation’s largest unions for health care, janitorial, security and other service workers.

National leaders had removed the head of a health care workers union in Northern California and appointed Mr. Regan to take over. The ousted leader started a rival organization, causing an ugly rift.

A lawsuit from that period accused Mr. Regan of threatening to call ICE to deport Latino home care workers if they did not vote to join his union. Nathan Selzer, a spokesman for Mr. Regan’s union, S.E.I.U.-United Healthcare Workers West, said the allegation was false and that Mr. Regan has long supported immigrants. The suit was settled in 2016.

Mr. Regan soon came to see how he could use California’s direct democracy system to negotiate for his members or needle his adversaries. In California, anyone can place a measure on the ballot by collecting enough signatures, and few people have been as skilled at it in the modern era as Mr. Regan.

“Regan is a specialist in using the referendum system,” said Nelson Lichtenstein, a labor historian at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “That’s sort of been his modus operandi.”

Mr. Regan has spent millions of dollars in union funds to collect signatures for dozens of ballot measures over the years, many of them to increase wages for hospital workers or limit compensation for health care executives. Often, the measures never appeared on a ballot because Mr. Regan withdrew them after getting concessions from employers or policymakers.

Other times, his measures have thrust California voters into obscure health industry fights, such as three propositions to regulate dialysis clinics. Another measure he got onto the November ballot, Proposition 44, would control spending by community clinics.

His measures often fail, but by appearing on the ballot, they force adversaries to spend millions of dollars on opposition campaigns.

“It has been a reign of terror and threats,” said Francisco Silva, head of the California Primary Care Association, an umbrella group for the clinics that would be restricted by Proposition 44.

Mr. Silva’s group recently filed a lawsuit accusing Mr. Regan of coercive and extortionist practices by using ballot initiatives as leverage. The suit claims that Mr. Regan offered to withdraw Proposition 44 if Mr. Silva’s organization were to endorse the billionaire tax and donate toward it.

“You’re not supposed to use the ballot measure that way,” Mr. Silva said. “You’re exchanging something of value, money, for using the ballot measure as a threat.”

In a statement, Mr. Regan’s union said that the allegations were false and that the clinics’ association had used lawsuits to “bully” union members into backing down.

The ballot measure, the union said, “will increase transparency, reduce wasteful executive spending and ensure clinic health care dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.”

Mr. Regan said in an interview that he was proud of using ballot initiatives to improve conditions for workers.

“Direct democracy is just a tool that’s available to us,” he said. “I still wonder why it doesn’t get used more.”

Mr. Regan has faced accusations of rough behavior over the years that went beyond his negotiating tactics.

In 2016, police in the San Francisco Bay Area said that Mr. Regan had pushed a process server who came to his house to deliver legal documents. In 2018, a state lawmaker reported being shoved by Mr. Regan outside a reception in Sacramento. Neither incident resulted in criminal charges, and Mr. Selzer, the union spokesman, said the allegations were false.

A 2018 lawsuit alleged that Mr. Regan oversaw a workplace where women were harassed and discriminated against, though he was not named as a defendant. Mr. Selzer said the union fired the employee who was accused of sexual harassment and Mr. Regan was not implicated. The lawsuit was settled in 2020.

Suzanne Jimenez, Mr. Regan’s chief of staff, has worked with him for 15 years and said that she had never seen him be physically rough.

“I will say, though, that he is direct,” she said. “He is focused on winning, not just for our members but for workers as a whole.”

Ms. Jimenez described him as a visionary who has helped to spread the use of ballot measures to progressive organizations in other states and successfully pushed for a significant minimum wage hike in California a decade ago.

Mr. Regan’s aggressive push to win support from other unions for the billionaire tax prompted investigations by at least two separate S.E.I.U. organizations. Their findings, first reported by The Los Angeles Times, have resulted in internal charges that will be heard in December by S.E.I.U. International, which has the power to punish him.

One of the most serious allegations surfaced during a conversation among several Democratic strategists and union officials who had gathered at a hotel bar in Sacramento after a holiday party hosted by Mr. Newsom in December.

Courtni Pugh, one of the strategists, told the others that Mr. Regan had physically assaulted her in 2009 when she was executive director of the S.E.I.U. California State Council. Ms. Pugh’s account was described in the investigations of Mr. Regan that the union commissioned this year. She declined to comment.

“Regan forced his way into her office, pinned her against the wall, and had his hands either around her neck or on her neck,” one report says, detailing the account that Ms. Pugh gave to her associates that night at the bar.

The other report said the 2009 altercation began when Mr. Regan was upset with Ms. Pugh’s handling of a ballot measure. It described Mr. Regan kicking her office door open, shoving her against the wall, pushing his finger into her chest and screaming an insult at her. She collapsed and began hyperventilating, the report says.

A colleague, Terry Brennand, found Ms. Pugh on the floor of her office and helped her get home. Mr. Brennand said in an interview with The New York Times that he had never seen Ms. Pugh so traumatized. He said he offered to testify for a workplace investigation but was never contacted until this year.

“There has been a lack of accountability in the entire process,” he said.

Ms. Pugh left the union and went on to build a successful career as a political consultant. She is currently working on campaigns for Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, and against the billionaire tax.

Mr. Regan said the 2009 incident never occurred and he accused Ms. Pugh of making up the story for political gain.

“She is a paid operative for the billionaire campaign,” he said. “It’s completely fabricated. Not a word was breathed apparently for 17 years until we’re doing this campaign and she stands to benefit.”

Another S.E.I.U. leader accused Mr. Regan of suggesting this year that the state council could be reported to the Trump administration for unspecified labor violations if it didn’t endorse the billionaire tax, one of the investigations said. That official described feeling “extorted,” according to the inquiry.

The state council ultimately decided not to take a position on the billionaire tax.

S.E.I.U. International, which oversees the state council and local unions, including Mr. Regan’s, plans to hold a hearing in December to evaluate the allegations that have emerged in the dust-up over the billionaire tax. That process will determine if Mr. Regan will face discipline.

“All sides will have the opportunity to present evidence and be heard,” April Verrett, president of S.E.I.U. International, said in a statement.

Mr. Regan said he is not worried because the allegations against him are not true.

“This is just character assassination and a smear campaign in a political context,” he said. “So we’ll get to the bottom of all of that.”

Since the accusations surfaced, several labor leaders have denounced Mr. Regan. Some lawmakers are calling on him to resign and the California Nurses Association said that it was “long past time for him to go.”

Eliseo Medina, who retired after decades as a senior official with S.E.I.U. and still commands respect in the organization, said the union must hold Mr. Regan accountable if the allegations are substantiated in the upcoming hearing.

“There’s no room for any leader in the labor movement that behaves in that manner,” Mr. Medina said.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Military Boards Are Defying Orders and Letting Trans Troops Serve
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a slur to proudly announce to an auditorium of Marines in September that he was ridding the military of all transgender troops.

The Pentagon had set up review boards at bases around the globe, manned by everyday uniformed service members with narrow orders that all but ensured that the trans troops appearing before them would be voted out.

But just steps from the auditorium where Mr. Hegseth spoke, at Marine Corps Base Quantico, boards assigned to carry out those orders were doing the opposite. Instead of firing trans Marines, the boards were voting to keep them.

The same was happening in the Navy: Boards given strict rules instructing them to force out sailors were rebelling and voting to let them stay.

It is not just a few outlying individuals. Navy and Marine Corps boards have voted to retain trans members in nine of 12 cases.

The Pentagon keeps the proceedings secret. Outsiders — even spouses — are not allowed to attend. Officials won’t release numbers. Leaders won’t discuss the outcomes. The New York Times compiled the figures through interviews with service members and lawyers involved in the hearings.

The number of Navy and Marine cases is small and could easily change as more hearings are conducted. The same pattern has not been seen so far in the Army or Air Force, which have overwhelmingly voted to discharge trans service members.

Still, the votes are a stunning rebuke from the armed forces, where following orders is bedrock. And they suggest the military’s transgender ban is being rejected by the very troops the administration says the ban is meant to serve.

“These boards are being told to do something that they know is wrong — to rubber-stamp a non-choice given to them by the administration,” said Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer and a professor at Southwestern Law School who has been tracking the cases. “We are seeing them say they’re not going to play that game. We are seeing them nullify a process they see as unjust.”

The board decisions are only recommendations, and could be reversed by the politically appointed secretaries overseeing each service branch. There are also pending legal challenges that could pause the ban or rescind it entirely.

The Trump administration claims that trans troops, who account for about 4,250 people or about 0.1 percent of the military, are a costly burden on military effectiveness — a position that military findings contradict. President Trump signed an executive order barring trans troops during his first week in office, saying the action was needed to weed out dishonorable radicals who poison morale and waste resources.

“For the sake of our Nation and the patriotic Americans who volunteer to serve it, military service must be reserved for those mentally and physically fit for duty,” the order read.

The Pentagon designed a policy that paid transgender troops to leave voluntarily. Hundreds of highly qualified people left, including doctors, lawyers, pilots and nuclear technicians. The troops who stayed to challenge their dismissal waited in limbo, sometimes for more than a year.

While they waited, the administration set up a system of three-member separation boards to process the remaining cases using a narrow set of instructions. Under the rules, any evidence of transgender feelings or tendencies — even if there is no formal transition — requires dismissal.

The three-person boards are made up of everyday officers and enlisted personnel plucked temporarily from their normal jobs to hear one case, like civilian jurors. They are not allowed to consider whether a person is a top performer, a specialist in a critical career field or a decorated combat veteran.

The members are given a one-page findings sheet and instructed to circle a few words to find that a service member exhibits evidence of being transgender and therefore is not qualified to serve and should be discharged.

At least, that was the plan.

Trans Marines and sailors who went before boards said in interviews that after months of being vilified by top government officials, they expected a quick dismissal, but instead encountered thoughtful respect from fellow service members who voted to keep them.

Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras was one of them. The Marine Corps pulled him from his job and put him on paid leave in April to await his discharge. In late August the Marine Corps flew him from Hawaii to Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia to face a board.

He walked in with his head down, sure that his career was over.

The government's lawyer presented documents from 2017 showing that he had changed genders.

The three members then reviewed his decade of flawless service as a supply and logistics specialist, his three overseas deployments, and his good performance reviews.

They then crossed out instructions on their findings sheet regarding “a history of cross sex hormone therapy” and circled “remains qualified,” and voted to retain him.

“I was shocked at first, but when you come down to it, it makes sense,” Sergeant Contreras said in an interview from Hawaii, where he is stationed. “You have war fighters looking at war fighters,” he said. “They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules. They say, ‘Hey, this is a good Marine, why wouldn’t we retain him?’”

Sergeant Contreras’s lawyer, Priya Rashid, has represented dozens of trans service members and has a broader understanding of the boards than anyone else. After losing nearly all of her initial cases, she saw a stark shift this summer. She has no idea why.

The Army was the first to hold hearings, beginning in February. It has held about 50, according to Ms. Rashid, and voted to discharge soldiers in all but about five cases.

The Air Force started this summer. It has reviewed about six cases and voted to discharge in every known case.

But the Navy and Marine Corps, which began holding hearings in July, have voted to retain in the majority of cases.

“I don’t understand why this pattern is occurring,” Ms. Rashid said in an interview. “And I’m worried that if the pattern becomes too apparent, the government will just change the processes and procedures again so that the pattern can be extinguished.”

Last week Ms. Rashid won another — this time in the Army.

Across the military, the hearings follow a pattern. A lawyer for the government briefly presents medical records and other documents showing evidence that a service member is transgender. The defense then often spends hours presenting a portrait of a service member’s years of service and accomplishments, submitting binders of awards and evaluations, and calling witnesses to vouch for character.

“It all made no difference,” said Maj. Kara Corcoran, an infantry officer who has served for 18 years and deployed to Afghanistan twice. An Army board voted in May to dismiss her in what she called a “kangaroo court.”

“They cut off my character witnesses halfway through and said, ‘We get it, your service is commendable, that’s not what we’re here to decide,’” said Major Corcoran, who now heads the trans advocacy group SPARTA Pride. “The government lawyer, the board, they thought it was ridiculous, but I think they felt they had no choice.”

Navy and Marine Corps hearings have followed the same pattern. But their decisions have been an about-face.

In the Navy, which began hearings in July, nine boards have led to seven votes to retain sailors, according to lawyers involved in the cases.

In the Marine Corps, which began hearings in August, three boards have led to two votes to retain. In the third, the board voted to dismiss a Marine, but wrote on the findings sheet that its members unanimously believed that the Marine should “be retained based on his commendable service record and unique skills.”

What’s driving the shift is far from clear. The military branches, citing ongoing litigation, declined to discuss the outcomes or make board members available for interviews. The Defense Department also declined to comment.

Ms. VanLandingham, the former military lawyer, said the votes might be influenced by growing concern in the ranks that the current Pentagon is preoccupied with wedge issues and gives little thought to the welfare of the force.

Mr. Hegseth in his speech to the Marines, she noted, said the force should have “No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals," but did not mention those killed or wounded in the war with Iran.

“There’s been a chipping away at any kind of confidence that Hegseth actually cares about service members,” she said. “I think that’s given the boards license.”

There may be cultural factors, too, she said. The board instructions in all the branches are nearly identical. But each branch has different values. The Army is often seen as the most bureaucratic and least likely to buck orders. The Navy is the most diverse. The Marine Corps prides itself on a culture of loyalty.

The Navy has nearly twice as many people who identify as gay, bisexual or transgender — 9 percent — compared to other branches, according to a 2015 report by the RAND Corporation.

That was clear to a Navy paramedic who was retained by a board in July. The paramedic, who asked to not be named because he feared retribution, said he was stunned when his lawyer asked a chief, a lieutenant commander and a commander sitting on his board if they knew any trans sailors.

“They all said yes,” the paramedic recalled in an interview. “The chief said his liberty buddy in Thailand was transgender and was a phenomenal sailor. The lieutenant commander said her first work center supervisor was transgender, and she learned a lot from her. The commander said he’d worked with several transgender sailors, and he barbecues with his next-door neighbor, who’s trans.”

There were other factors working in his favor. He had been meritoriously promoted twice for superior performance; remained able to deploy his entire five years in the Navy; and had saved several lives working in emergency rooms.

For his last assignment he was attached to Marines deployed to the southern border. “I never ran into people who cared if I was trans,” he said. “They just cared that I did my job well.”

His lawyer, Steph Kral, a former Air Force officer, represented a second sailor a short time later in front of a different board that she said had no relationships with trans sailors. That board also voted to retain.

“I don’t think they are trying to make any grand policy statement,” Ms. Kral said. “I think they’re just trying to do what’s best for the Navy.”

The Marine Corps has the lowest reported percentage of women, gay and transgender personnel. It also has a tradition-bound culture based on masculine toughness. But Marines have an almost cultlike loyalty to fellow Marines, expressed in their motto, Semper Fidelis — Always Faithful.

“The questions from the Marine boards have focused in on how the policies of higher-ups may have changed, but the Marines in question never did anything wrong,” Ms. Rashid said. “I think they are looking for a way to give a fellow Marine the benefit of the doubt.”

When Sergeant Contreras went before a board, he produced years of performance evaluations and letters from superiors — some who never knew he was trans — that vouched for his good work.

After deliberating for about three hours, the board scratched out language on the instructions sheet about evidence of being transgender and voted to let him stay.

“It was very humbling to see the things that they had to say about me,” the sergeant said. “It had nothing to do with being transgender. I honestly don’t think they care about that. It was about how I was a great Marine.”

item.title: The Michigan Senate Race Keeps Getting Nastier
item.description:
Mike Rogers snickered as his surrogate smeared his opponent.

At a recent campaign stop at a winery an hour outside Detroit, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana told a scrum of reporters that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan and a Muslim, sleeps in an Osama “bin Laden jersey.”

Mr. Rogers, 63, swallowed a sip of his water and smiled. He is a former Army officer, F.B.I. agent and representative who headed the House Intelligence Committee until his term expired in 2015 after he opted not to run for re-election. Even Democrats considered him levelheaded and cooperative — “a voice,” as one lawmaker put it, “for moderation and consensus building.”

Now, though, Mr. Rogers is running to be the first Republican senator from Michigan in a quarter century — and running in a political era fundamentally different from the one in which he came of age. As the United States lurches toward Election Day, this race has come to embody the spiraling toxicity of the country’s politics.

While any of a handful of other competitive Senate contests could help determine the new balance of power in Washington, none comes close to matching the mounting racial and religious menace and meanness in Michigan. President Trump has taken to calling Dr. El-Sayed, a former public health official, a “jihadist.” When Dave Portnoy, a provocative internet celebrity, called Dr. El-Sayed a “terrorist,” Mr. Rogers was quick to respond. Mr. Portnoy, he said on social media, “is exactly right.”

Roxie Richner, a spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed, called the attacks on him “heinous.” He is “as Michigan as it gets,” she said.

Abby Ronson, a spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers, said Dr. El-Sayed was the one “spewing hate.” She cited his response to a Hezbollah-inspired attack on a Michigan synagogue that critics deemed insufficient and insensitive and for which he subsequently apologized. She also mentioned a comment in which he said when his opponents go low, “we take them to the mud and choke them out.”

Allies of Dr. El-Sayed dismiss any notion of equivalence. Ravi Mangla, a spokesman for the Working Families Party, which has endorsed Dr. El-Sayed, called the discourse from Mr. Rogers and his supporters “deeply racist and Islamophobic.”

Back at the winery in Highland Township, Mich., in a barn that had a dirt floor and smelled like horses, speakers rallied a crowd of more than 900 people wearing cowboy boots and MAGA hats. Many questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s patriotism.

“He’s a citizen, but that does not make him an American,” said David Beamer, the father of Todd Beamer, the leader of the passengers who thwarted the terrorists who hijacked Flight 93 on Sept. 11, 2001. “He’s not an American.”

“We believe in this country,” said Kristi Rogers, Mr. Rogers’s wife. “Our opponent does not.”

“We will save this country if we win this election,” Mr. Rogers said to rising hollers and applause. “The whole country is watching!”

As the ugly rhetoric at Mr. Rogers’s campaign events has escalated, so, too, has a palpable sense of peril at those of Dr. El-Sayed.

One recent evening in Western Michigan, a group of far-right activists crashed a campaign stop in rural Oceana County, thrusting wooden crosses into the air and chanting that Dr. El-Sayed needed to be “deported.”

“This is our country!” Jake Lang, an influencer and provocateur who was pardoned by Mr. Trump after going to prison for his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot, bellowed into a bullhorn. “We will not be Islamified!” (Mr. Rogers has called Mr. Lang a divisive, violence-promoting “fringe extremist.”)

“Go home, dirty Arabs!” another man yelled.

The next afternoon in nearby Muskegon, in a downtown theater before a crowd of 1,400, Dr. El-Sayed stood on the stage in front of a Michigan flag and an American flag and between two bodyguards.

“Now, look, I’m not supposed to run for office,” he said.

“I’ve got the wrong name,” he added. “Apparently, I pray the wrong way.”

A burly man got up out of his seat near the front of the room. He was wearing hightops, sweatpants and a baggy white shirt with the image of a red Templar cross from the Crusades. He advanced toward Dr. El-Sayed.

The bodyguards moved toward him.

A campaign staffer confronted him.

“Let him talk,” Dr. El-Sayed said.

“The problem is,” the man said loudly, “his book says something different than my book.”

Dr. El-Sayed, 41, is the son of Egyptian immigrants and his first language was Arabic. He grew up mainly north of Detroit, raised mostly by his father and stepmother.

In the Democratic primary, Dr. El-Sayed campaigned with Hasan Piker, the incendiary anti-Israel streamer who recently told Axios that the United States “pound for pound” was responsible for more terror than Al Qaeda. Dr. El-Sayed has distanced himself from Mr. Piker but has not fully disavowed him.

At a debate earlier this month Mr. Rogers sought to tie Dr. El-Sayed and his family to Hamas, Hezbollah, Al Qaeda and the Muslim Brotherhood, part of a broader effort to make insinuations of such associations a central issue in the stretch run of this race. Afterward, Dr. El-Sayed was asked why he didn’t dispute those claims. “This is about trying to point to somebody whose name is different,” he said. “I’m just not going to dignify it.”

Since then, though, Dr. El-Sayed has pushed back, disavowing the Muslim Brotherhood during a town hall event over the weekend and in an exchange with a reporter from Newsmax.

In Muskegon, at the theater, Dr. El-Sayed talked to the man with the cross on his shirt.

“I’m grateful that you’re here,” Dr. El-Sayed told him. “Do you follow canon law?”

“Vaguely,” the man said.

“I would recommend as a Christian that you go read canon law,” Dr. El-Sayed said, “because it is supposed to pattern your life choices as a Christian. Here’s the thing about it: Because of the U.S. Constitution, you have the right to live according to canon law — and also because of the U.S. Constitution, you don’t get to enforce canon law on anyone else. You pray as you choose to pray, I pray as I choose to pray.”

The rest of the answer was all but drowned out by a deafening ovation. The man began to point and wave his hands. The cheers turned to jeers.

“Get him out of here!” people shouted.

“U.S.A.! U.S.A.!” Dr. El-Sayed said, and the crowd followed. “U.S.A.! U.S.A.!”

Three police officers approached the man and led him up the aisle and toward the door, and he turned amid the ruckus and his thumbs up switched to middle fingers.

In speeches, Mr. Rogers calls himself a “proud son of Michigan and a product of the American dream.”

He grew up as one of five brothers in rural Brighton Township and helped pay for college by making Chryslers on car lines. He was in the Army in California. He worked for the F.B.I. in Chicago.

He was a state senator in the late 1990s before running for Congress in 2000. He won, by 88 votes, on an anti-negativity platform. “I’m not asking you to vote against my opponent,” he said in an ad. “I’m asking you to vote for me.”

He represented his mid-Michigan district for seven terms and became the Intelligence chair. He was a mainstay on political television shows after the rise of the Tea Party helped Republicans reclaim control of the House in 2010.

But he tired of the intensifying polarization and “brand identity politicians” doing the “celebrity thing,” he said at the time. In his last speech in Congress, he appealed to colleagues and citizens to “find the better part of our angels.”

He signed with Cumulus Media and Westwood One to do talk-radio commentary. In contrast to Rush Limbaugh or Sean Hannity, Mr. Rogers hoped there was space for “a more productive, you-might-actually-learn-something kind of talk radio,” he said at the time.

“I’m a bit of a canary in a coal mine,” he added. “I am hoping I don’t choke on the fumes at the bottom of the shaft.”

He was a national security commentator for CNN. He joined corporate boards to advise technology and cybersecurity firms.

He founded Americans for Peace, Prosperity and Security, putting on foreign policy forums featuring 2016 Republican presidential candidates like Lindsey Graham and Marco Rubio.

In 2020, Mr. Rogers warned that it was “exceptionally dangerous” that Mr. Trump was refusing to acknowledge that he had lost the presidential election. And in the aftermath of Jan. 6, he said it was “damn right” that Mr. Trump “had responsibility.”

In 2022 and 2023, Mr. Rogers explored the possibility of a presidential run of his own. “Trump’s time has passed,” he said in The Washington Post. “Angry and scary is not a way to win elections,” he said in New Hampshire.

Two years ago, though, Mr. Trump urged Mr. Rogers to run for the Senate. He lost by just 19,000 votes to Elissa Slotkin, the centrist former C.I.A. analyst and official for the Department of Defense.

This year, against a very different political opponent in a very different political environment, Mr. Rogers is working to put together a fragile and complicated coalition. He needs the MAGA base, Republicans who have soured on the president and small but sufficient slices of voters who typically pick Democrats — including Jewish and Black voters.

On the campaign trail, Mr. Kennedy, the senator from Louisiana, summed up the Michigan race in simple — if vulgar — terms.

“Mike Rogers pisses excellence,” Mr. Kennedy told reporters outside a factory he and Mr. Rogers toured. Dr. El-Sayed, he said, is part of “the Hamas wing of the Democratic Party.”

Mr. Rogers was asked if Mr. Trump’s continuing use of Dr. El-Sayed’s middle name — Mohamed — is a dog whistle “gone too far.”

“I can’t pick the guy’s middle name,” Mr. Rogers said. “It’s his legal middle name. My argument is maybe — his middle name — we should change it to ‘that big government socialist.’”

Ms. Ronson, the spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers, said that his campaign would not use such loaded language. “But we’re also not going to speak for the rest of the Republican Party, and we’re also not going to speak for the president.”

At the barn at the winery in Highland Township, after his speech, Mr. Rogers huddled with half a dozen Black women. They hugged him and posed for pictures. Together they bowed their heads and prayed.

Why, they were asked, were they voting for Mr. Rogers?

“If you’re going to hold office in America,” said Valeria Berry of Detroit, “you need to be an American.”

]]>

item.title: Most Voters Believe the Midterm Elections Will Be Accurate, Poll Finds
item.description:
With less than two weeks until the midterms, a wide majority of voters say that they largely trust that the results of the upcoming election will be accurate, according to a new New York Times/Siena poll. But the poll finds that many harbor concerns that Republicans could try to overturn the results of the election.

The findings come as President Trump has frequently sought to sow doubts about the integrity of elections, and as his administration has pushed unfounded claims of rampant fraud in the voting system and warned of its potential manipulation by foreign powers.

But nearly three-quarters of voters said they trust the accuracy of elections, including large majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents. A small but growing share of voters said that they do not trust that the results will be accurate, though: 23 percent now say this, the poll found, up from 17 percent who said the same of the 2024 presidential election.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 12-19

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 3,494 likely voters nationwide conducted Oct. 12 to 19.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

“Elections have always been fair and accurate for the history of the United States,” said Jonathan Wall, a 62-year-old lawyer living in Greensboro, N.C. “ I truly believe that the results will be counted accurately.”

Mr. Wall, a Democrat, said that even as he personally believes the election will be fair, he worries about fake accusations being made about the elections not being accurate.

Half of likely voters said that they were worried about the possibility that Republicans might try to overturn the results of the November election through illegal means. By comparison, 31 percent of voters said they were worried about Democrats doing the same.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 12-19

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 3,494 likely voters nationwide conducted Oct. 12 to 19.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

“I never had too many thoughts about an election being stolen until Donald Trump came into office,” said Kristina Sterling, a 56-year-old interior designer living in Denver. “I’m not a conspiracy theorist, but it just makes me nervous with the amount of crazy things that have gone on.”

Ms. Sterling, an independent, said she had voted Republican for most of her life but has leaned more toward Democrats in recent years. She said she worries about the results this fall. “I don’t even know what Republicans could do to mess with the election, but it scares me that they could do something,” she said.

Eighty-six percent of Democrats and just over half of independents expressed concern that Republicans would try to overturn the results of the election through illegal means.

Then there is the question of who gets to vote in the first place. In the run-up to the midterms, the Trump administration has sought to prioritize purging noncitizens from state voter rolls, even though experts say that instances of noncitizens voting are extremely rare.

A majority of voters said they were more concerned that some eligible voters would not have a chance to vote than about the possibility of voter fraud. That is a reversal since 2024, when voters were more concerned that some people would cast votes illegally.

The party divisions on that question are stark. While 85 percent of Republicans said they were more worried that some people would cast votes illegally, 86 percent of Democrats said they were more worried that some eligible voters would be deprived of their vote.

There were some areas of agreement across the political divide. Concern about the future of democracy is shared by both Democrats and Republicans. More than three-quarters of voters said that they think American democracy is under threat, a number that has remained largely consistent since 2022.

For all the polarization and vitriol of the current moment, most voters said that they did not view members of the opposing party as “the enemy.” Large majorities (78 percent of Republicans and 75 percent of Democrats) said that they viewed members of the opposing party as fellow Americans they disagree with politically.

But the share who sees the other side as “the enemy” has grown. About 22 percent of Democrats now say they see Republicans as the enemy, up from 20 percent who said Mr. Trump’s supporters were the enemy in 2024. And 20 percent of Republicans now say the same of Democrats, up from 15 percent who said the same of former Vice President Kamala Harris’s supporters in 2024.

Voters are uniformly worried about this growing divide. Nearly 60 percent say the country is too divided to solve its problems. That is a reversal since September of 2020, when a majority of voters said the country can still address its problems.

“So many people lose friends over this,” said Gregg Blanchard, 54, a political independent living outside of Houston, Tex. “I have friends across the political spectrum. But I think that’s increasingly rare.”

Here are the key things to know about this New York Times/Siena poll:

You can see full results and a detailed methodology here. If you want to read more about how and why we conduct our polls, you can see answers to frequently asked questions and submit your own questions here.
